Karl Frank  
26 Primrose Gardens  
London, N.W. 3  
September 27, 1939.

Dear Friend,

I would like to carry on a correspondence with you. You will understand that all of the news I can get is of great interest to me at this time. I also promise to send you news about our friends, etc.

I should like to describe our situation to you briefly. Here they have set up Tribunals before which the foreigners from countries at war shall appear, by which it will be decided whether or not they are to remain free. With the help of our friends we have gotten sufficient legitimations so that we expect to be granted a certain amount of liberty. After this, please do not write to the address that you used before the war but to me, or still better to my wife, Anna L. Frank, at the address given at the top of the letter. Will you write me regularly, knowing how important every bit of news is to me. I should also be very grateful if you could let me have clippings from the Swedish press that are really interesting and of course any clippings you might be able to get from German papers. Naturally, everything must be censored here, but that no longer involves the long delay of the first days of the war. We even hope that it may be arranged that the post comes through more quickly than normal for us.

We have transferred the publication of the "Informationsbrief" to New York. It will be printed there and you will receive it as soon as possible. I plan to remain here in England myself, but hope to get permission for a trip to New York and back, in order to carry on my work.

The situation of our friends in Paris has been less favourable. Paul Hertz, Berbhard and some of the others are already at liberty. I imagine you are able to get in touch with mx Pforten at any time. Will you send copies of any news you are able to send me to Mary Fox in New York for our editorial committee there.

With best wishes,

Sincerely yours,

Karl Frank
